list.listitem: Primary closure of clean, well-vascularized wounds is generally appropriate within 24 hours for head/face/scalp and often within 12–18 hours for other clean wounds. However, no single evidence-based time cutoff is well-defined, and the decision should incorporate contamination, wound characteristics, and patient risk factors.
Delayed closure of contaminated full-thickness skin wound or greater than 12 hours after injury.
Deep wounds of the hand or foot.
Full-thickness lacerations of the eyelid, ear, or lip.
Lacerations involving vessels, bone, tendons, joint, or nerves.
Penetrating wounds of unknown depth.
Severe crush injuries or severely contaminated wounds that may require drains.
Wounds leading to a strong concern for cosmetic outcome.
Need for patient sedation.
Open fractures.
Involvement of salivary duct or canaliculus.
Any wound the attending physician feels uncomfortable repairing.
For irrigation: sterile saline, sterile water or tap water for irrigation, 18 gauge angiocatheter, 25 to 50 cc syringe, 4 x 4 sterile gauze.
For local anesthesia: 1% to 2% lidocaine or 0.25% bupivacaine, 8.4% sodium bicarbonate for buffering, 18 gauge needle for drawing, 25 to 30 gauge needles for injection, 3 to 10 cc syringe.

A Cochrane review found low-quality evidence supporting the effectiveness and safety of topical anesthetic preparations, as an alternative to infiltrated local anesthetics, for pain control during dermal laceration repair.
Obtain laceration history including mechanism of injury, elapsed time, tetanus immunization status, and possible allergies to local anesthesia, latex, and antibiotics.

Surgical hand antisepsis with chlorhexidine gluconate reduces the number of colony-forming units (CFUs) more than povidone iodine scrubs, but the clinical significance of this as it relates to postop surgical site infection (SSI) is unclear. 3-minute initial scrub appears better than a 2-minute scrub, again mostly based on the disease-oriented outcome of CFUs. It is unclear if nail picks and brushes are helpful. All included studies in this Cochrane review have been deemed low to very low quality evidence.
Prior to beginning the repair, thoroughly examine the wound for foreign bodies, depth, involvement of tendons, nerves or vessels and assess neurovascular status.
If preoperative hair removal is necessary, use clippers instead of razors as the latter increases SSIs, based on moderate-certainty evidence from a Cochrane review.

Irrigate wound with copious sterile saline, sterile water, or potable tap water (evidence is low certain; effects on infection are uncertain) through an 18 gauge angiocatheter to cleanse at 5 to 8 lb per square inch of pressure without damaging the tissue. Povidone-iodine, hydrogen peroxide, and detergents should not be used due to their toxicity to fibroblasts.
Debride any foreign material and non-vitalized tissue.

Use 1% to 2% lidocaine or 0.25% bupivacaine for local anesthesia. Solutions with epinephrine may be useful to decrease wound bleeding and are generally safe in digits in patients without compromised perfusion; use caution in patients with significant peripheral vascular disease or other perfusion concerns. Total safe local anesthetic doses are 3 to 5 mg/kg for lidocaine without epinephrine, up to 7 mg/kg for lidocaine with epinephrine, 1 to 2 mg/kg for bupivacaine without epinephrine and up to 3 mg per kg for bupivacaine with epinephrine.
Use 1% diphenhydramine (1 ml of diphenhydramine 50 mg/mL solution in 4 mL sterile saline) for those allergic to amide forms of local anesthetics.
Decrease sting with local anesthetic injection by warming the solution, buffering with 8.4% sodium bicarbonate (1-10 mL of local anesthetic) using a 25- to 30-gauge needle, and injecting slowly.

Lidocaine 1%/epinephrine 1:100,000 (Lido/Epi) buffered with sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) in a 3:1 ratio is less painful during infiltration compared to unbuffered Lido/Epi and buffered Lido/Epi in a 9:1 ratio.
Cooling the anesthetic injection site with an ice pack reduces pain and discomfort caused by the injection without statistical difference in wound infection risk (n=90, P<0.001).

Perform the laceration repair using sterile technique including sterile gloves and fenestrated drape. Clean nonsterile gloves do not appear to increase infection rates, however. Adhesive drapes have not shown benefit and may increase SSIs in clean surgery; they are not routinely recommended for simple laceration repair.

Choose closure technique (below) depending on the location and size of wound, potential skin tension, available materials and physician experience. Suturing remains the gold standard, but other techniques are as good in certain situations such as adhesive tapes for shin wounds, hair apposition technique (HAT) for scalp lacerations, and tissue adhesives over skin wounds having low tension, i.e., face and backs of hands.

Equipment needed: gloves (sterile gloves do not reduce risk of infection over nonsterile) , fenestrated sterile drape, 5 mL syringe, 18 gauge (for drawing up local anesthesia) and 25- to 30-gauge (for injection) needles, needle holder, rat-tooth forceps, small straight hemostats, appropriate absorbable and non-absorbable sutures (3-0 to 6-0), scissors, 4 x 4 gauze pads.
Suturing is the gold standard technique for laceration repair.

Non-absorbable sutures, such as nylon monofilament (Ethilon), polypropylene, and silk, may be used to close the superficial layers of the skin. The use of silk or cotton sutures in wounds with significant bacterial burden should be avoided.

Absorbable suture, such as polyglactin 910 (Vicryl) polyglycolic acid (Dexon) and poliglecaprone 25 (Monocryl), are traditionally used to close deep layers to eliminate the potential space and decrease wound tension and for tendon repair. They may have a role with superficial closure on the face or with pediatric patients as well with similar wound dehiscence rate, cosmetic results and infection risk to non-absorbable suture.

There is uncertainty whether subcutaneous closure using absorbable sutures, compared to no subcutaneous closure, is helpful in decreasing postoperative complications (eg, dehiscence, hematoma, etc.). Subcutaneous closure has the potential to increase operative times.

Subcuticular sutures appear comparable to transdermal sutures, staples, tissue adhesives, and surgical tapes in terms of postoperative SSIs. Subcuticular sutures result to less wound complications compared to staples and have better patient satisfaction compared to transdermal sutures or staples. However, tissue adhesives have better patient satisfaction than subcuticular sutures, while transdermal sutures and staples are faster to apply than subcuticular sutures. Evidence from this Cochrane review range from high to very low.
Antibiotic coated (triclosan) PDS suture does not reduce the occurrence of surgical site infections compared to uncoated PDS suture.

Use the finest suture possible, depending on skin thickness and tension, to achieve optimal cosmetic results. In general, use 3-0 or 4-0 for trunk, 4-0 or 5-0 for limbs and scalp, and 5-0 or 6-0 on the face (see ). Absorbable 3-0 or 4-0 suture should be used for mucosal lacerations.
Remember to enter skin with needle at 90 degrees to surface and twist the wrist to cause wound eversion which compensates for scar retraction with healing.
Choose appropriate suturing technique from single interrupted, running or "baseball" closure, subcuticular running closure depending on location, skin tension, and physician skill.
Use horizontal and vertical mattress suture techniques for areas of high skin tension.
Use half-buried mattress or "corner" stitch for closure of a triangular wound as it remains subcuticular in the flap, avoiding the blood supply and theoretically decreasing tip necrosis.
A trial randomized 50 patients to 2 mm vs 5 mm interval for a running cuticular closure and found no difference in any outcomes.
Sutures need to be removed depending on location ().
Equipment needed: gloves (sterile gloves do not reduce risk of infection over nonsterile), tissue adhesive (2-oxtylcyanoacrylate or like) ampule, smooth forceps, 2 x 2 gauze.

Tissue adhesives (i.e., 2-octylcyanoacrylate, Dermabond) are comparable with sutures in cosmetic results, dehiscence rates and infection risk with for appropriate wounds, such as those with low tension on the face, trunk, and backs of hands.

They are cost-effective with quick application, no anesthesia requirement, and elimination of need for follow-up as they slough off spontaneously in 5 to 10 days. This latter fact makes them ideal for lacerations under a splint or cast.

Tissue adhesives are contraindicated in patients with risk of poor healing (e.g., immunocompromised, diabetic) and should be not be used for wounds that are contaminated, complex, or jagged lacerations, mucosal surfaces, and in areas the maintain moisture such as the groin or axillae.

Tissue adhesives, based on low-quality evidence from a Cochrane review, appear inferior to sutures for the outcome of postoperative wound dehiscence but similar to sutures as far as rates of postop infection, cost, and physician and patient satisfaction. They should be avoided for high-tension surgical sites.
Wounds should be dried after irrigation and placed in a horizontal position to control runoff, especially around the eyes.

Approximate wound edges with gloved fingers or forceps, then apply the tissue adhesive over the wound with a five mm overlap on each side. Be sure not to apply the adhesive in the wound, but over it. Repeat every 30 seconds until three to four layers are applied.
Avoid antibiotic ointment and petrolatum ointments as they remove tissue adhesives.

Use HAT for non-bleeding scalp wounds less than 10 cm long in hair greater than 3 cm in length. Bring opposing hair strands together, twist and apply tissue adhesive, holding until dry. This technique causes less scarring, has fewer complications, and is more cost-effective than scalp suture repair.

A recent systematic review of ED traumatic wound closure techniques similarly found comparable outcomes across closure methods for appropriately selected wounds, with differences mainly in procedure time, pain, and dehiscence risk in higher-tension sites.

section.type: Laceration Repair Technique: Stapling and Skin-Closure Strips
section.heading: Laceration Repair Technique: Stapling and Skin-Closure Strips

list.listitem: Use staples for thick skin on extremities, trunk, and scalp; avoid face/neck for cosmetic reasons and avoid hands/feet and over highly mobile joints where tension/motion increases dehiscence risk.
Do not use stainless steel staples for scalp wounds if neuroimaging of head is anticipated.
The quick application of staples makes them ideal for multiple trauma or intoxicated patients.
Use skin-closure strips for small, simple lacerations in low-tension areas with well-approximated edges, but be aware of potential wound dehiscence due to lack of tensile strength.
Use skin-closure strips for pre-tibial lacerations as they have faster wound healing and less tissue necrosis.
After laceration repair, clean wound with sterile water, apply antibiotic ointment (if no tissue adhesive used) and sterile dressing.

It is unclear if applying dressings after primary closure of surgical wounds reduces SSIs, nor is it certain if any dressing is better than others in preventing SSIs, minimizing scarring, decreasing pain, improving patient satisfaction, or facilitating easy removal. Additionally, early removal (within 48 hours) of wound dressings from clean or contaminated surgical wounds does not appear to affect important outcomes, based on very low quality evidence.

For minor contaminated wounds, topical triple antibiotic ointment decreases infection rates when compared with petrolatum. For sterile wounds, however, pertrolatum is equivalent to triple antibiotic ointment in decreasing infection rates. A Cochrane review concluded that topical antibiotics, based on moderate-certainty evidence, appear more effective than no topical antibiotics or topical antiseptics in preventing SSIs in wounds healing by primary intention. There is uncertainty regarding whether topical antibiotics increase adverse events like contact dermatitis or on its impact in the development of antibiotic resistance.

Routine systemic prophylaxis is not recommended for uncomplicated, clean lacerations; reserve antibiotics for high-risk wounds (e.g., gross contamination, devitalized tissue, bites) or high-risk hosts.

There is uncertainty whether early postop showering or bathing (<48 hours after surgery) is better or safer than delayed postop showering or bathing in preventing surgical wound complications. A single-blinded RCT involving 437 adults found no difference in complication rates with water exposure at 6 hours versus 48 hours after cutaneous surgery.
Give discharge instructions including wound care, signs of wound infection and suture removal timing, (see ) if appropriate.
Based on a single RCT in 45 people, botulinum toxin type A may reduce scarring.
Local bleeding post-repair usually responds to direct pressure and dressing changes. If persistent, re-opening of wound to control actively bleeding vessels may be necessary.

Wound infection usually occurs approximately 3 to 5 days following the laceration repair. After evaluation, consider removal of sutures or staples to allow closure by secondary intention. Consider appropriate antibiotics to cover common skin flora if cellulitis or systemic symptoms are present.
Wound dehiscence occurs from tissue strain or premature removal of suture/staples. No treatment is necessary except for reassurance and wound dressing.
Recheck repaired laceration only if concerned about potential infection, i.e., contaminated or bite wound, or other neurovascular issues.
Refer to plastic or orthopedic surgery wounds that involve tendons, bones, nerves, or vessels.
Return for suture removal at appropriate interval ().
